analysis.one_liner: Lets federal health officials regulate tobacco like other dangerous products, with bans on sales to minors and free samples.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 1989 with bipartisan support but never got a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority over tobacco products under federal food and drug law. It would have banned selling tobacco to anyone under 18, banned handing out free samples and discount coupons, required companies to disclose all additives and test each brand for tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide, and replaced one warning label with a blunt statement that smoking is addictive. It died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, especially minors who are the target of free samples and coupon promotions. The bill's own findings cite research that 60 percent of new smokers start before age 14, and it aims to keep tobacco out of the hands of children and to tell adult consumers exactly what is in the products they use.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal offense to sell tobacco products to anyone under 18, and lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services impose stricter rules on how and where tobacco is sold in states that fail to enforce the ban [S2][S3].
Bans distributing tobacco as free samples or through coupons and other discount promotions, a marketing method aimed at hooking new users [S2][S3].

Requires manufacturers to disclose every additive in their products and to have each brand tested and labeled for tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, and other harmful constituents before it can lawfully be sold [S2][S3].
Replaces the carbon monoxide warning with 'Smoking is Addictive. Once you start you may not be able to stop.' [S2][S3]
Treats any nicotine-containing product that is not tobacco as a drug under federal law, closing a loophole for substitute products [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, importers, and packagers, who would bear testing costs, additive disclosure, new warning labels, and the loss of free-sample and coupon marketing. Retailers would face new restrictions on the form, manner, and location of tobacco sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill layers a new federal regulatory and testing apparatus on top of existing tobacco laws, and compliance would fall first on manufacturers and retailers; critics of tobacco regulation have argued this creates costs without making smoking any safer, since the product remains legal and harmful regardless of what the label says [S2][S3].

Enforcement of the under-18 sales ban is left mainly to the states, and federal rules on sale location and manner only kick in after the Secretary finds a state's enforcement insufficient, so the bill's core promise to minors depends on state governments acting [S3].

Additive limits and constituent rules are set by the Secretary's judgment with expert advice, which invites years of rulemaking, litigation, and lobbying before any actual reduction in harm reaches consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: tobacco was, by the bill's own findings, the single most preventable cause of death in the United States, and its promotion to children was legal and routine. The cost is a new regulatory burden on manufacturers and retailers and a slow, discretion-heavy enforcement path. On balance, the bill asked a large, profitable industry to accept disclosure and youth-sale rules that the industry had avoided for decades.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and it never came back out for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Bob Whittaker of Kansas introduced the bill on March 20, 1989, joined by 15 other House members as original cosponsors, including Mike Synar, Dick Durbin, Barbara Boxer, and Ron Wyden [S3][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over tobacco [S5].
On April 3, 1989, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where legislation typically goes before any committee vote [S5].
No further action was taken. The bill never received a committee markup, a House floor vote, or action in the Senate, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers, who kept an essentially unregulated product: no federal additive disclosure, no constituent testing, and free samples and coupon promotions to potential new customers remained lawful. That benefit was preserved without anyone having to vote against the bill on its merits.

for.name: Rep. Bob Whittaker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 27 cosponsors across both parties [S1][S4][S5].

for.name: Rep. Mike Synar and 14 other original cosponsors
for.role: House members, mostly Democrats plus Republicans Collins, Nielson, and Shumway
for.what_they_did: Signed on at introduction, giving the bill 16 original sponsors and eventually 27 cosponsors [S3][S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tobacco, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or a vote; the bill sat first in the full committee, then in the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers and marketers of cigarettes and smokeless products
against.what_they_did: Maintained and expanded a roughly $2 billion annual promotion effort that the bill would have restricted, and had a long record of fighting federal regulation of tobacco [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan (19 of 257 House Democrats and 8 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored), but no Republican or tobacco-state member moved it out of the Democratic-controlled committee, and no floor vote ever happened [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced disclosure of additives, government testing of every brand for tar and nicotine, new addiction warnings, a ban on free samples and coupons, and possible bans on additives. Its own findings noted tobacco was one of the least regulated consumer products despite $2 billion a year in promotion, so the industry's interest ran directly against the bill's consumers.

Sellers would face a federal ban on sales to minors and possible federal rules on the form, manner, and location of sales in states with weak enforcement. Compliance costs would fall on retailers, though the burden targets sales to children specifically.
Free samples, coupons, and discount promotions were the marketing tools the bill outlawed outright, and new additive and constituent disclosures could be used against brands in advertising disputes.
